name: Aloe leaf extract

lead: Aloe leaf extract is a staple of after-sun gels, moisturizers, sunscreens and facial products. People use it to soothe and hydrate skin so it looks calmer and smoother.

The clear inner gel is mostly water and contains the polysaccharide acemannan. Wikipedia describes the evidence for burns and wounds as conflicting, and small registered trials are mostly in oral and gum conditions. None in the sources reviewed test cosmetic appearance.

paras: Applied as a gel or in lotions, commonly after sun exposure or as a light daily moisturizer on irritated or dry skin.

Topical use in small amounts is likely safe, with allergic reactions possible. Oral latex or whole-leaf extract is linked to cramps, diarrhea and hepatitis, and regulators have acted on aloin laxatives; the cosmetic limit on anthraquinones is 50 ppm.

angle.text: Aloe gel soothes and hydrates skin, so it looks calmer and smoother after sun or irritation. Evidence on wound healing is conflicting, and its effect on appearance specifically is lightly studied.

lead: Aloe leaf extract is a preparation from the leaves of Aloe vera, a succulent native to the Arabian Peninsula that has been used on skin for thousands of years, with Wikipedia citing records of skin use from the fourth millennium BCE [1]. In cosmetics it is a common soothing and moisturizing ingredient in lotions, gels, sunscreens, shampoos and facial products, where people use it to calm irritated or sun-exposed skin and keep it hydrated [1].

For looks, the chain people describe is simple: a water-rich, mildly acidic gel applied to the skin adds moisture and soothes redness or irritation, so skin looks and feels calmer, and some users apply it after shaving, sun, breakouts or minor cuts. The NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says clinical research suggests aloe gel may speed burn healing and reduce burn pain, and that two small studies suggest it may help acne when combined with other treatments [2].

The leaf yields two main materials. The clear inner gel contains the polysaccharide acemannan, while the yellow latex contains aloin, an anthraquinone with laxative properties that is considered toxic [1]. The cosmetic industry limits anthraquinone content in aloe extracts to 50 parts per million [1]. Wikipedia describes the evidence for burns and wounds as conflicting, and says topical use in small amounts is likely safe with allergic reactions possible [1].

paras: Aloe gel is added to lotions, soaps, moisturizers, tissues and makeup, and is traditionally applied to minor burns, abrasions, insect bites, windburn and dry skin.[1] Cosmetic companies value it for a moisturizing emollient effect.[1] The gel is mildly acidic, with a pH of about 4.4 to 4.7, which can cause burning or rash on irritated skin.[1] Whole-leaf extracts and latex-containing products differ from decolorized gel in anthraquinone content, which is the basis of most safety regulation.[1]
Besides acemannan, the leaf contains other phytochemicals such as lignans, phytosterols, polyphenols, anthrones, emodin and lectins.[1]

Aloe vera is a perennial with thick, fleshy grey-green leaves edged with small white teeth and yellow tubular flowers; it is hardy in warm climates and needs well-drained soil and infrequent watering, which is why it is a popular houseplant as well as a crop [1]. Linnaeus first described the species in 1753, and some researchers suspect it is of hybrid origin [1]. Aloe gel is also used in yogurts, drinks and desserts, and aloe latex has historically been used as a laxative [1].

Aloe is a widespread after-sun and soothing ingredient and appears in simple routines for sensitive or irritated skin. On T Nation, a member recommended a 100 percent aloe gel product as a moisturizer and sunscreen option in a thread asking for moisturizer suggestions, and other members mention aloe gel alongside calendula cream for wound care and, in one thread, fresh gel from a real plant for discoloured skin.[3][4][5]

Typical uses described for appearance are after-sun soothing, a light moisturizer or base under sunscreen, post-shave calming, and as an ingredient in acne and redness products. Gel from the plant is also applied by hand, and forum users distinguish between bottled gel and fresh leaf gel [3][5].

Looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums mention aloe in several side roles. One T Nation member noted that aloe gel and isopropyl alcohol were still in stock when commercial versions of a product sold out, and described them as the ingredients for making your own [6]. Another described adding about a tablespoon of fresh leaf gel to a morning shake, saying it was good for the gut [7], and a user described mixing a compound with aloe gel and DMSO as a transdermal preparation [8]. These are personal reports rather than research findings.

Wikipedia reports early records of aloe use from the fourth millennium BCE and a mention in the Juliana Anicia Codex of 512 CE; it was introduced to China and parts of southern Europe in the 17th century.[1] Today it is grown at scale in countries including Australia, Mexico, China, India and South Africa, with much output going to the cosmetics industry.[1]

Wikipedia's history places the plant's origin around the Hajar Mountains of Oman and the UAE, with introduction to China and southern Europe in the 17th century and later naturalisation across North Africa and the Canary Islands [1]. Large-scale cultivation now serves mainly the cosmetics industry [1].

In a laboratory comparison, aloe vera gel extracts showed antibacterial activity against bacteria associated with skin infection, tested alongside antibiotics.[9] In a mouse model of chemically induced skin tumors, oral aloe leaf extract and topical aloe gel were reported to reduce the number and size of papillomas.[10] These are in-vitro and animal findings.

Wikipedia lists acemannan, lignans, phytosterols, polyphenols, anthrones, emodin and lectins among leaf constituents [1]. NCCIH notes that most animal safety studies used non-decolorized whole-leaf extract, a form consumers do not commonly use, and that a 2023 review found drinkable products with no more than 10 ppm aloin were not genotoxic [2].

Topical use of small amounts is likely safe, and allergic reactions such as contact dermatitis can occur.[1] Taking latex or whole-leaf extract by mouth has been associated with abdominal cramps, diarrhea and hepatitis, and chronic ingestion with other harms; aloe may interact with drugs including anticoagulants, diabetes medications and digoxin, and Wikipedia advises against use during pregnancy.[1]

The US FDA banned aloin-based over-the-counter laxatives in 2002 after manufacturers did not provide adequate safety data. California listed non-decolorized whole-leaf extract as a chemical known to cause cancer on December 4, 2015, and since 2016 the IARC has classified whole-leaf extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B).[1]

NCCIH describes topical aloe gel as generally well tolerated, with occasional burning, itching, rash and eczema; short-term oral gel for up to 42 days appears safe in research, while oral latex can cause cramps and diarrhoea and oral leaf extracts have been linked to cases of acute hepatitis [2].

Registered trials test aloe gel mainly in oral and dental contexts: aloe vera against chlorhexidine for traumatic oral ulcers in 140 participants (phase 4, started 2015) [11] and aloe vera gel compared with clindamycin gel as an addition to scaling and root planing for periodontitis (30 participants, 2023) [12]. Results are not posted in the registry records.

On skin, NCCIH reports clinical research suggesting aloe gel may speed burn healing and lessen burn pain; two small studies suggesting benefit in acne when combined with other treatments; and a small body of work on psoriasis, lichen planus, radiation skin damage and herpes, with insufficient information on eczema and diabetic foot ulcers [2]. Wikipedia says evidence for topical use in burns and wounds is conflicting and that topical use may ease symptoms of psoriasis, acne and rashes [1].

Recent reports include a split-face randomised trial of 30 people with acne erythema in which topical aloe vera gel and a dual-wavelength laser both significantly reduced redness with no significant difference between them (response at 8 weeks was 69 percent for aloe and 72 percent for laser; the laser acted faster) [13]; a split-face study of 10 patients after upper-eyelid blepharoplasty that used aloe-treated and untreated eyelids to examine early scar markers and later satisfaction [13]; and a 2024 single case report of pure aloe extract on a superficial second-degree burn, with epithelialisation in 11 days against an expected 14 [13]. A 2025 review of herbal creams in dermatology associates aloe vera with anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and wound-healing effects and flags irritation, contaminants, variable concentrations and weak regulation as concerns [13]. Laboratory studies report antibacterial and anti-tumor-promoting activity of aloe preparations [9][10]. No trial identified tests aloe leaf extract on facial attractiveness outcomes.
